title: Dizzy as pathfinder; melody, pit jobs and Black players
summary: Dizzy changed the instrument like Hawkins, but followers cannot play melody, and Black musicians are excluded from pit bands and hotel jobs; Butler complains of Fiedler and Lawrence Welk.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: When you heard people like Dizzy play the trumpet, were you as impressed by him as you were by Armstrong around, when you heard Armstrong in his prime?

No. Dizzy -- Dizzy man, everybody knows that. He changed the instrument. He changed -- he changed that instrument. He was the first one. He changed it. See? He changed the whole panorama -- he changed it. See, he was a pathfinder.
That's -- like Coleman Hawkins. Coleman Hawkins changed that instrument. This instrument was hawking and going on and it was -- it didn't -- it was ugly, cumbersome.

Now, you listen to some of those old records -- the man was playing beautiful but it was heavy and uneven. So, I mean, that's because -- like you -- see, you cats, you cats in-between trumpets. Dizzy is inbetween trumpet.
See, Dizzy, Dizzy, Dizzy said, I'm going to go my way -- so did Lester Young. Said, I'm going my way.
Uh-huh.
See? And and, and, you got so many fellows they was going to follow Dizzy and they can't play a melody.
Huh.
And, and, and, -- those other people, they was happy about that.
Uh-huh.
And that's why they wasn't getting no jobs in the band, in the pit. They can't play no melody. They can't play no melody.
And there was a time when Dizzy had nothing but bands of color in these hotels.
Uh-huh.
Them people went and told them that -- they can't play melodies, so therefore, and they believed it. All they can do is get them strange sounds.
Uh-huh.
Them awful sounds. And right today, they go -- oh, he don't know music. He can't play in the pit.
Uh-huh.
Like this man up here in Boston, up here, with all those musicians up there, you don't have nothing black up there, around up there.
Fiedler?
Yeah. So, he ain't moving me at all. I'm talking about Lawrence Welk.
Oh, yeah.
Ain't no one playing the trumpet, the trombone -- and the percussion, he ain't got nobody, and he want
to make me like him. So -- he don't move me.
